utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. The Chamber has convened today to determine the status of this matter and the course of its preparation for trial. Now, Mr. Stanisic, are you able to hear me in a language you understand? He hasn't a microphone. Are you able to hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's important that you be able to follow the proceedings this morning. Now, appearances. For the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Anna Richterova; to my left is Karen Beausey; and to her left is Sooraya Gareeboo; to my right is Crispian Smith, case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bezbradica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Stevo Bezbradica, and still official counsel for Mr. Mico Stanisic, who is present in this courtroom this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The matter we're dealing with, of course, has not been formally called and it might be useful for the record if that were now done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-79-PT, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since the last time that there was a Status Conference in this matter, which was on the 9th of January, there have been developments particularly recently which caused the Chamber to have considerable concern as to the potential for this case not to be ready for trial. Let me make it clear that this is one of three cases that will be commenced during the second half of this year and could be called upon to commence as early as late July. The situation, of course, is that three trials are in their final stages, and when those trials finish, the next three cases will necessarily have to be ready to proceed. And this one is one that has been waiting for some time, it's important that it proceed, and we want to be sure that things are in order for that to happen. What particularly caused the Chamber concern is the issue of the representation of the accused, Mr. Stanisic. There have been difficulties with the present Defence counsel and his payment, and then there was a formal notification by the accused that he wished to represent himself and not to continue with the present representation. The position that concerns the Chamber is that while that is happening the capacity of Mr. Bezbradica to properly and adequately represent the accused is obviously being adversely affected. He is not currently receiving the normal instructions that he would receive, and there is apparently not the normal communication that there would be between counsel and the accused. Given the need to ensure that certain critical matters which remain to be dealt with in the final preparation of this case are dealt with and dealt with properly so that the trial is ready and the accused's Defence in particular is ready for trial, the Chamber felt it important that we look closely at this issue of the representation of the accused. To that end, it appeared to the Chamber essential that the accused be present here for these proceedings and orders were made for his return to The Hague for that purpose from the provisional release that had previously been in place. The Chamber is informed that following yesterday's hearing before the principal Legal Officer that Mr. Stanisic had discussions yesterday with representations of the Office of Legal Aid and with the Deputy Registrar of the Tribunal. Can we take this moment, Mr. Stanisic, if I address you fairly directly to point out to you the very great significance that there is for you in ensuring that you are adequately represented and that your defence is properly prepared and properly presented. I don't think we need to emphasize to you the importance of the issue of whether you are found guilty or not guilty of the charges that are being brought against you. It is obvious that if you have a significant defence, that should be properly prepared and presented during the trial. It's also the case that the trial can be expected to take many months. It will not be, we hope, one of the enormously long trials that can occur in this jurisdiction; but it is still a trial that can be expected to take in the order of a year. It may finish more quickly than that if all parties are well prepared and the issues are focused on clearly, but it's going to be, even with that, a trial of some length in which you will be called on to be in court normally five days a week, which is the sitting practice of this Chamber, for example; and that means that witness after witness will come, you will need to be prepared to deal with that witness, to present what needs to be put to that witness, and to prepare your own witnesses and have them ready when the time comes. I see that you did graduate in law some years ago, but I gather that you've not been practicing law. Your interests have been mainly elsewhere. And frankly, the task of keeping up with the pace of a normal hearing is simply too much for one person. If you were to be representing yourself, the consequence would be that some of the things that you would want to do in the preparation and presentation of your defence could not adequately be done because you would just not have enough time and energy to be able to do them as well as they ought to be done. Now, if you were representing yourself, the Trial Chamber would do what it could to try and ensure that your case was being adequately presented. But in the end, the responsibility of the Chamber is to do two things: To give you an opportunity to present your case properly, but also to ensure that the trial is finished as efficiently and as quickly as possible. We can't just let the case drift on at a pace that you find comfortable. This Tribunal has had to conduct a number of trials where accused people have sought to represent themselves, and we've been learning from each one of those cases how better to deal with the problems that they often present. No two cases are the same, that's obvious, but one thing that we have learnt is that it is just not fair to anybody, least of all the accused, but certainly not to the other accused waiting to be tried, to allow the case to just go at a pace that is so slow that one accused can adequately present the defence. So it cannot be the case that you can expect to be able to handle the case in your own time, in your own way, and we want you to be very aware of that. You want and you need and you ought to be able to ensure that your case is presented as adequately and soundly as possible, and that is obviously very much in your interests. It's also in the interests of this Tribunal to try and ensure that the trial is fair and the issues are fully presented, and it's also in the interests of everybody to ensure that that can be done as quickly and efficiently as possible so that the trial can be shorter and a final decision, whether it be not guilty or guilty, is reached as quickly as possible. For that reason, the Chamber would suggest to you very, very firmly that it would not be in your interests to be representing yourself and trying to take the load of conducting your own defence alone throughout the trial. You need competent assistance. You will be busy but with others doing some of the work as well, it is in that way possible to keep up with the pace of the trial, to be prepared for each of the witnesses, and to have your own case ready. Therefore, the Chamber was very gravely concerned at your advice that you wished to conduct your own defence. We would urge you to consider that position very carefully, and we would put to you that really you are putting yourself at risk of not being able to put your case properly, no matter how the Trial Chamber tries to help if you do not have legal representation to help you. Now, you are aware and it's common knowledge that you have been provided with counsel to assist you under the legal aid scheme of this Tribunal. One issue is whether you wish to change counsel at this time. It is getting very near the end of the preparation of your defence and there are obviously problems about changing counsel at this point, and this Chamber has to look carefully at any proposal that you have. It is the case, though, that it could be open to you if your mind, for whatever reason, is clear that you would like to have other counsel assigned, that it would be possible for you to choose other counsel from the lengthy list that is available of counsel who are able to appear here who are experienced counsel. Now, the Chamber does not want to go into the questions of your relationship with the counsel who's represented you now for, I think, over two years and who has been conscientiously performing that responsibility. But if it is the situation that you are clear in your mind now, for whatever reason, that you want some other counsel to represent you, well then that needs to be dealt with quickly and decisions made in fairness to the preparation of your defence, in fairness to your present counsel who has been carrying on with great difficulty in recent months, and in fairness to whoever you choose to be your new counsel because they must now pick up a case and under some time pressure get prepared themselves and become fully familiar with your case. So we are putting to you the situation I hope very clearly. A, that if you really want to represent yourself you would be doing yourself harm, you would not be putting forward your best case. And we would have to consider very carefully as a Chamber whether we could allow that to happen. We would urge on you the view that you really do need to be represented in the conduct of your trial because that way there is the best chance that all the matters favourable to you will be put forward in the best way. If it is the case that what you want to do is to be represented but by some other counsel, that should be dealt with - we would suggest - during this week; it can't just run on as it is at the moment. So we would take the position that we would ask the -- you've lost the translation, have you? Is it back again? Thank you. We would take the position that we would ask the Deputy Registrar, Mr. Hocking, to continue discussions with you with the head of the legal aid office of this Chamber, with a view to resolving in the next days of this week finally whether your present counsel is to continue or whether you wish another person to be assigned or what it is. And the Chamber will, if necessary, reconvene this Status Conference later in the week to deal with the matter further. We would like you to consider your position in light of what we have been saying now, in the hope that you can reach decisions which will enable your case to be properly presented with the assistance of counsel that you are happy to have go forward to present your case through the assistance of the legal aid scheme that is available here. And we want you to reach your decisions, taking into account what we've tried to indicate to you briefly about the difficulties and disadvantages of the sort of course you were contemplating. It's not right to ask you now to make decisions. You ought to have some time to think about it further, and we will arrange for the Deputy Registrar and the legal aid office head, Mr. Petrov, to speak to you again and discuss possible arrangements. And because of that we would also invite Mr. Bezbradica to remain in The Hague during the next few days of this week, with a view to the matter being finalised. It may be that there will be a clear decision that you continue; it may be there will be a clear decision that some other counsel be appointed, and we would hope that that can be arranged, even in the course of today, if not then in the course of tomorrow. The Chamber will be here sitting in another case and we'll be able to convene at short notice, if necessary, to assist further in that matter. Have you been able to follow what we've been suggesting so far to you, Mr. Stanisic, about the need for some final decisions to be made about what you wish to do, and depending on those decisions the Chamber may have to consider further particular orders. But we'll look at that after you've had time to reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's been pointed out to me, Mr. Stanisic, that you nodded that you had understood what we were saying and that you would give the matter consideration, but you didn't say so and so the record doesn't reveal. If you have understood what we are saying and will think about the matter, perhaps you could just indicate yes, you will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all I would like to thank the Trial Chamber which showed understanding three years ago and issued a decision on my provisional release, and thus allowed me to adequately prepare for the upcoming trial. All the changes that have occurred in the meantime I claim will not have a bearing on any of the dead-lines in preparing my defence because I've been actively working for three and a half years now with a team of advisors who are in Belgrade, and we have also taken Mr. Bezbradica on board occasionally through e-mail. We have not been able to contact him in any other way. I can promise you at this point that I will reflect on my position and the option whether to represent myself or to take another counsel, but as far as Mr. Bezbradica is concerned I don't want to waste any of your time but my final conclusion is that I cannot accept him as my Defence counsel. Maybe there will be an opportunity to go into the detail of that decision, but maybe this is not a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is not a good time, and the Chamber would make clear to you, Mr. Stanisic, that it will be for the Chamber to make that decision because you are in a position where you're receiving legal assistance. And we have to try and ensure that your trial is conducted fairly to you, and the step of simply saying, I want to represent myself, has such potential adverse implications for your defence that this Chamber would have to give very careful consideration to whether it would allow that move. And that's why we have been, A, trying to make you understand some of the difficulties that lie ahead for you if you were to want to go down that course; and also why we have been very genuinely interested in urging upon you the course of considering, if it is that you wanting to change counsel, to make that decision and have some other counsel appointed as quickly as possible because that will then enable this Chamber to accept that your defence is again being adequately prepared and will be ready to be properly presented. So I hope that's a little more clear to you now. It's not the case at this stage, in the last stages of preparation for trial, that you can simply say without more, No, I'm going to represent myself, because our responsibility is to ensure for you a fair trial and an efficient and speedy trial. It might preclude us from agreeing to that course. Well, if you could look at that question of counsel in the next day or so as soon as you're contacted again, we would be very grateful. And what we will now do is to move on to quickly canvass some other matters and -- yes, Mr. Bezbradica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you turn on the microphone. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, because I interrupt you, but you mentioned a few minutes ago that I need to stay a few days further in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does this create a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because when I came in I didn't know for your -- for this new point that I need to stay here. I already booked only for three days here, and tomorrow I'm going back. I have my obligations there in Melbourne, I didn't know. It was easy for me to book few days to stay here before I know for this Status Conference; it's really hard for me to do that now because I really need to go back there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What time tomorrow is your flight?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Departure time is 12.00 a.m. you know, at this moment I'm really doing really hard work because at this stage I have to cover up everything, and I did that. It is really hard to stay here because I have to go there to finish some necessary job for me who is -- which is a connection with my office there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have a notice from your written communications, Mr. Bezbradica, that you have been experiencing some difficulty gaining instructions about various matters. Would you be in a position to indicate to the Chamber how you feel the relationship is at that moment? Are you in a position to continue, as it were, to conduct the defence of the accused or is this a matter which you find has become impractical or impossible?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As you are aware, I am in this case since the 5th of May, 2006, and two days two years. On the 5th of March, Mr. Stanisic asked for my withdrawal from the case, and already my submission to the Tribunal, and the Registry already explained reasons why I thought that accused -- that Mr. Stanisic's allegations are not correct to me and I did explain that. From the beginning we had really good communication to each other -- especially I have really good communication with him. Now something is coming back. And my intention is not to repeat everything what's happening and my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, we're not asking you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: No, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We just want to know where you find yourself at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: At the moment I don't like, Your Honour, to represent him before the Tribunal for -- I think that our relationship, because of his allegation, there is already broken and cannot be reconciled under any condition. I don't know what will be your decision. If you decide that I must go there and that -- you know, I will obey your decision, but it will not be my free will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're grateful for that indication, Mr. Bezbradica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's one of the factors the Chamber must take into account as it deals with the decisions reached by Mr. Stanisic as he reflects on this matter. We're grateful for that. We will work on the basis that you will be departing tomorrow on a flight at noon and it may be that some final indication of your position can be given by then, otherwise that communication to you will be in your office in Melbourne. So thank you for your preparedness to be here and for the indication you've given. If the Chamber could now move on, there is a motion for leave to amend the indictment from the Prosecution which was one of a number of motions which for a time this Chamber had thought better left for the actual Trial Chamber that would conduct the trial, when it appeared likely that that would be another Trial Chamber. Circumstances have changed with the progress of other cases and the availability of Chambers, and it's clear now that we need to deal with these final matters relevant to the preparation of the case for trial, even though at this moment it's not possible to be certain exactly when this case will begin and before which Chamber. So we are giving attention now to those matters which have been held. And the question of the amendment of the indictment has come back into sharp focus. We did give a decision early in April, which called upon the Prosecution to reconsider the indictment with a view to limiting its scope, that is, to lessening the range of allegations in the indictment. The Prosecution has made, as we requested, a response to that, in which it proposes the removal of some particular allegations but does not in any way diminish the charges that are brought and the essential range of what is alleged in what the Prosecution now proposes is substantially that that was there before. There has been the identification of some particular sites or locations that could be removed, but they still leave, even if those changes were made, a very wide-ranging indictment. And because of that, the Chamber is of the view that it should look fully and carefully at the question of whether an order should be made by the Chamber pursuant to Rule 73 bis, which would be more effective in lessening the range and scope of the present indictment. For that reason, Ms. Richterova, the Chamber would ask that in 14 days from now, within 14 days from now, that you might present formal submissions pursuant to Rule 73 bis about the indictment. We would make it clear that the Chamber has no fixed or final view about this matter, but we are concerned that what is presently alleged is very wide-ranging and it may be that the essential issues of the case from the point of view of the Prosecution can be adequately dealt with in the smaller, more confined indictment. And therefore, we must ask you to put in more detailed submissions so that the Chamber can reach a view whether it ought to order the reduction of the indictment more than was proposed in your response made a couple of weeks ago. There will be a formal order published to that effect, but it will be with a view to submissions being made by the Prosecution within the next fortnight. Is that time, do you think, adequate for your purposes? We fixed on it, having in mind that you have just looked at the indictment and come up with proposals so that a lot of the work and thought has already been dealt with and we were of the view that probably a fortnight then was a fair and adequate time for you. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think two weeks could be adequate time; however, if Your Honour allow me to address just very briefly few points. I think it is important to consider our 24th April submission in combination with our previous submission, our submission in relation to presentation of evidence pursuant to 92 bis, 92 ter, also on 29 of February we filed our amended list of witnesses. And we have reduced the time of presentation of our case quite significantly. We reduced it from 243 hours to 175 hours, and if you take into consideration our proposal from 24th of April when we suggested, first, to remove completely certain seven of crime sites or incidents plus we proposed not to lead any evidence on 76, approximately 76 other crime sites and incidents. Together it is already over 100 sites for which we don't intend to lead any evidence, which is half of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Half of the incidents, yeah. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've looked at that, and of course what you're now doing is possibly part of the submissions you would make under 73 bis. We're aware of it, but we feel that it is a case where we should explore fully whether the indictment can sensibly and properly be reduced further, and we would therefore like your full and reasoned submissions about that. We don't lightly see it as our role to step in and limit the indictment just arbitrarily; we want to give you a proper scope for presenting your case. But when we look at what your case presently is, what you propose your reduced case should be, we think we have reason to look more closely and fully at whether it can be reduced even further. So we'd be grateful if you would do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Of course we will try to do our best. We -- I only would like to know whether Your Honour suggest that we file a proposed amended indictment in which we would incorporate all suggested changes. Because at this moment we have our 9 May motion, 14 February motion to amend the indictment. Now we proposed another scope -- reduction of the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have a rough working document which probably does that, but as Judge Thelin points out there may be some misunderstandings or uncertainties about that and it would be a wise precaution if you were to file a -- your understanding of what you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So, yes, it is a useful and helpful suggestion, we're grateful for it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. And we will file it within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I make it clear, Mr. Stanisic, so that you're aware with Mr. Bezbradica as to what is happening. The Chamber has called on the Prosecution to think of reducing its indictment, making it smaller, removing some of the allegations against you. The Prosecution about two weeks ago made some proposals to make the indictment smaller. The Chamber has said to the Prosecution, We, the Chamber, wants to look more closely at that to see whether the indictment can be made even more smaller, whether we can reduce the indictment more. From your point of view, any reduction in the indictment will be to your advantage. The Chamber is doing it from the point of view of trying to ensure that the essential case against you is presented but not with unnecessary breadth of allegations and range of issues. We want to get down to what really is the essential case, and for that reason we are asking the Prosecution now within another 14 days from now to look again to see what matters might or might not be further reduced out of the indictment. The Chamber will then decide whether the indictment should be further reduced or not in light of those submissions. So understand that's what's happening. We're seeing whether the indictment can be made smaller, which will lessen your task in defending if that should happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is also now looking at a new third motion by the Prosecution for judicial notice of previously adjudicated facts to be taken. The Chamber has given some decisions about these matters already, and the Prosecution has now moved firstly a third motion on the 25th of January this year and then a fourth motion on the 24th of April this year, proposing further adjudicated facts and those motions will be now considered and dealt with by this Chamber. There is a proposal to amend the witness list by the Prosecution. It removes some witnesses, proposed the addition of some others, and of course that is affected by the actual indictment. If the indictment were to be reduced, that list may have to be further amended. But the Prosecution has proposed presently, at present, that there be a change to it Rule 65 ter witness list; and we have had responses from the Defence about that and we will give consideration to that. And that applies not only to its motion of the 29th of February but also its further motion of the 25th of April. There is a motion for protective measures for certain witnesses which the Chamber will deal with, and there are also motions for the Prosecution to be able to present part of its case from a number of witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater, which are forms of written evidence with or without cross-examination, and also pursuant to Rule 94 bis, which deals with expert witnesses. Now, those matters are also now to be dealt with by the Chamber. The only motion from the Defence which the Chamber presently has is one concerning remuneration of assigned counsel which was filed on the 9th of April and which we will give consideration to. The Chamber has asked the parties to explore agreed facts. We understand that the position is that there has been no agreement reached, proposals having been made by the Prosecution; the Defence has not responded positively. This was dealt with last in the Status Conference in -- on the 9th of January this year. At the moment, from the point of view of the Chamber, that is a matter which will have to await a resolution of the Defence counsel position because this does call for positive decision by the Defence whether to agree certain facts and at the moment change of counsel will perhaps affect the approach taken to that. So at the moment the Chamber is working on the basis that there is no present prospect of agreement being reached on any of the proposed facts. The point of all this, if I can make it clear, Mr. Stanisic, is that there are often matters which can be agreed because there are facts that the Prosecution wants to be accepted and there are facts that the Defence doesn't dispute. If they can be agreed, it means that some witnesses don't have to be called and can speed up the trial. So it's a matter that is useful for focusing on what really is in dispute in the trial and ensuring the trial can proceed as quickly and efficiently as possible. So once there's been resolution of the Defence counsel position, we would ask that there be a sensible look at proposals for agreed facts because it's in your interests, as well as the Prosecution, that if there are facts that aren't disputed to have them formally agreed. I wonder --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- address this issue. I would like to clarify certain points. There are some agreements. If Your Honour remember in your decision from December in relation to adjudicated facts, certain facts were transformed into agreed facts. In addition to these facts, there was communication between the Prosecution and the Defence about additional agreed facts, and we managed to reach a limited number of agreed facts. However, when we proposed a consolidated list of these agreed facts, the negotiation was stopped and the Defence refused to communicate any further. So this is one clarification which I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. I think you had proposed some 60 facts, and it was thought that perhaps 26 facts might have been agreed. But it -- all of that, as we understand it, is now not moving forward and we think resolution of Defence counsel issue first may then enable the issue of agreed facts to be looked at again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was about to turn to you, Ms. Richterova, to ask whether there are any difficulties now being experienced with disclosure and how that is progressing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This issue was addressed yesterday during 65 ter conference. I do not have any problem -- or better say I hope Mr. Bezbradica expressed that he has received all our disclosure. And if he was missing something, he always addressed first the Prosecution. So I think the disclosure -- there is no problem regarding the disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that your understanding of the position, Mr. Bezbradica?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Everything is correct what Ms. Richterova said. In due time -- at the moment I'm receiving all CDs necessary for this procedure, but only now at the moment because this situation is a little bit confused because of my request for my withdrawal. I don't know how can I provide Mr. Stanisic with everything. In -- since the 5th of March, when I received official -- his request for my withdrawal, in the two occasions I mailed by express post from Melbourne to Belgrade few CDs, in which each parcel, and by two occasions I have been confirmed by Australia post that Mr. Stanisic received that. The third parcel -- yesterday I spoke with Belgrade it has not been received by him because in the meantime he came back to The Hague now. Now I don't know how can I provide him with everything. Is it good that Prosecution directly provide him with that CDs or not. Maybe in the space of time they are going to mail directly to me to Melbourne and I have mail back to The Hague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're posing a couple of issues there. The first one is to ensure that anything you have presently received is communicated to Mr. Stanisic. And it seems there is one bundle still in the mail that hasn't been received by Mr. Stanisic. We will --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, and I understand -- I have been advised yesterday that when I'm coming back to home I have to make official request back to Melbourne everything and after that I should mail to him here. I haven't tried to provide him with two last CDs because I know that they can't reach him -- he is already here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you brought them with you or are they in Melbourne?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: I have it here, it is copies I have here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would expect it would be practical for you to make those available to Mr. Stanisic here so that you wouldn't have to trouble about mailing them, and we would expect that the one that you have mailed that have not yet been received you will be able to ensure is received by Mr. Stanisic. The second limb of your question is for the future, what happens about future disclosure to you. And I believe that will be resolved this week by decisions about the future representations and conduct of Mr. Stanisic's case. Because if it is the case that you do not continue as counsel, if that's the outcome, there will be no point in any further service made on you. It will be service on the newly appointed counsel or whatever is the arrangement. Okay. So that problem should resolve itself in the course of this week. The -- I know this week you've been inconvenienced, Mr. Stanisic, by coming to The Hague and I know that you now seek to have provisional release reordered. The Chamber will look at that, but we really need to get resolved this representational issue; and if things are then back on the rails we can look at the resumption of your provisional release. I take it you see no problem with your health, do you, at the moment with the trial continuing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You shook your head very firmly saying, No problem; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Problems with health is something I fear most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We share that problem. Very well. Well, the Chamber will look forward to hearing from you, Mr. Stanisic, progress in the consideration of this question of your representation, and we hope all of that can be finalised in the course of this week. Yes, Mr. Bezbradica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: I apologise, I made mistake, my departure time tomorrow is 12.00 noon, not 12.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood that, you're travelling probably Singapore airlines --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Malaysia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Malaysia, right. I knew the departure times. Very well. Now, is there any other matter that you feel needs to be raised, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are no other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bezbradica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZBRADICA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you already mentioned that Mr. Stanisic asked for his release from the detention, also from my side I also filed my motion on the 2nd of May. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. They will be considered and dealt with. Is there any other matter you want to bring up, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, except for putting in additional effort to resolve this problem, I don't have anything else I would like to raise right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanisic. Well, I hope that by the end of this week we'll have got everything resolved and the whole of the case back on track to be ready for trial hopefully even by the end of July. We will now adjourn. We would thank all parties for their attendance and assistance today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: adjourned at 11.10 a.m.
